questions.prompt: Which litter setup best matches the registered guidance for one cat?

options.text: One compact box beside the bowls so every resource is easy to find.
options.feedback: The arrangement is convenient for the owner but provides too few boxes and removes the physical separation between toileting and eating.

options.text: Two suitably large boxes with unscented litter, separated from food and water.
options.feedback: This is the best answer: one box per cat plus one extra, appropriate size and litter, and physical separation of resources.

options.text: Several small scented boxes moved regularly so Milo does not form a rigid preference.
options.feedback: More boxes alone do not solve unsuitable size, scented substrate, or unstable placement. Reliable use supports keeping a location stable.

questions.prompt: Which observation most strongly suggests marking rather than a full toileting event?

options.text: A small volume on a vertical surface while Milo stands with her tail raised.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Small-volume vertical placement and standing tail posture fit the registered marking pattern.

options.text: A full-volume elimination on a horizontal surface beside the litter tray.
options.feedback: This more closely resembles toileting outside the box. Volume, posture, and surface matter to the distinction.

options.text: Any urine outside the box, regardless of volume, posture, or continued box use.
options.feedback: Treating every event as one category discards the observations needed to distinguish marking, toileting, and location preference.

questions.prompt: Why should an owner avoid deciding that house-soiling is either medical or behavioural at home?

options.text: The categories can coexist, and treating one factor may not remove a learned aversion.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Medical and environmental factors can overlap, so professional assessment and careful observation both matter.

options.text: Behavioural causes are only considered after every possible disease has been permanently excluded.
options.feedback: Medical causes must not be assumed away, but the guideline does not require pretending environmental or learned factors cannot coexist.

options.text: The distinction is unnecessary because every case is managed by changing the litter setup first.
options.feedback: A setup change may be relevant in some cases, but using it as the universal first answer can delay attention to a medical cause.

questions.prompt: Which observed pattern should override a general wait-and-record approach?

options.text: One quiet afternoon after an unusually active morning, with normal eating and elimination.
options.feedback: This belongs in the record but does not match the narrow urgent urinary signature or another concrete warning sign by itself.

options.text: Repeated attempts to urinate with no output and crying during the attempts.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The observable pattern warrants immediate same-day or emergency veterinary care without waiting to identify the cause.

options.text: A preference for one of two clean boxes while both remain regularly used.
options.feedback: A preference can inform setup decisions, but it does not resemble repeated unproductive straining or inability to pass urine.

questions.prompt: Milo has not eaten for more than 24 hours and is unusually tired, but urinates normally. What should the owner do?

options.text: Contact the vet today and compare the appetite and energy changes with Milo's baseline.
options.feedback: This is the best response. Appetite loss and lethargy are registered warning signs even without the urgent urinary presentation.

options.text: Wait because normal urination proves the change is behavioural rather than medical.
options.feedback: Normal urination removes one presentation, not every health concern. It does not explain or cancel the appetite and energy changes.

options.text: Offer a favourite food and only contact the vet if Milo refuses it twice.
options.feedback: A food offer can add observation, but an invented two-refusal threshold should not delay contact after more than 24 hours without eating.

questions.prompt: Milo urinates outside the box after noisy repairs begin. Which first response is safest?

options.text: Punish the location once so Milo understands the box rule remains in force.
options.feedback: Punishment does not address medical, environmental, or learned causes and may add stress to a problem already associated with household disruption.

options.text: Record volume, posture, location, and other signs; keep boxes accessible and seek veterinary advice if warning signs are present.
options.feedback: This is the best response because it preserves medical-first reasoning while still noticing the real environmental change.

options.text: Assume the repairs explain the event and wait until they finish before recording or contacting anyone.
options.feedback: Noise is a plausible factor, but a plausible explanation is not evidence that no medical issue exists. The pattern still needs observation.

questions.prompt: Milo eats less, drinks more, hides, and shows slight effort in the box but produces a normal amount. Repairs are noisy. What is the strongest judgement?

options.text: Attribute the cluster to repair stress because normal urine output rules out concern.
options.feedback: The environmental explanation is plausible, but reduced appetite and increased thirst remain independently listed warning signs worth professional discussion.

options.text: Log the specifics and contact the vet today for guidance without labelling the case an obstruction emergency.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis: it acts on the warning-sign cluster while respecting that the narrow no-output emergency signature is absent.

options.text: Treat it as confirmed obstruction and attempt emergency relief at home before travelling.
options.feedback: The chapter teaches recognition and escalation, not diagnosis or treatment. Normal output also means the narrowly defined obstruction signature is not established.
